Industry and building types Company Size and Respondents’ Number of Years in Industry Contractors in the sample ranged from very small firms with only a few employees to larger companies with thousands of employees. Small (1–50 employees) and medium (51–200 employees) firms made up 63%, a significant portion of respondents, underscoring the importance of workforce strategies that are accessible to businesses with less administrative capacity relative to larger firms. 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR) at www.nlr.gov/publications. Growth aspirations were widespread, with 82% of all respondents reporting that they wanted to grow their companies. This desire was especially pronounced among small to medium firms, with 91% of companies with fewer than 50 employees and 95% of those with 51–200 employees expressing interest in growth, compared to just 65% of firms with more than 200 employees. These findings underscore the critical importance of tailoring business development and workforce initiatives to the needs of small- and medium-sized contractor firms, which represent a sizeable portion of the sector and have the potential to be the strongest drivers of future workforce expansion. Respondents reported a wide range of industry experience, from early-career workers to individuals with nearly five decades in the trades. Seventy-nine percent had at least six years in the industry, with 43% of total respondents having been in the industry for 6-10 years. This distribution suggests that the views captured by the survey are grounded in medium to long-term, practical experience with hiring, training, and managing workers. Interestingly, when comparing respondents’ experience with their reported age, about 39% of respondents in the 45–54 age bracket had less than 10 years of experience, suggesting late entry into the industry.
